introduction: At Henry VIII's court, advancement depends on royal favor, and apparent security can disappear in a moment. Cardinal Wolsey exercises immense influence over the king and the nobles, while Queen Katherine defends both suffering subjects and her place in a marriage increasingly questioned by Henry. As Anne Bullen attracts the king's attention, personal desire becomes entangled with diplomacy, church authority, and the succession. The play follows successive tests of loyalty and conscience through accusations, public ceremonies, and private confrontations.

fullSynopsis.text: The Duke of Buckingham condemns Cardinal Wolsey's pride, costly diplomacy, and political maneuvering, despite Norfolk's warnings about provoking so powerful an enemy. Buckingham is arrested for treason. Queen Katherine then confronts Henry with the distress caused by a heavy levy, which the king orders revoked. Wolsey privately instructs his secretary to credit him with the relief. Buckingham's former surveyor accuses the duke of imagining himself king and contemplating violence. Katherine questions the witness's motives, but Henry accepts the charges strongly enough to order a trial. At Wolsey's lavish entertainment, Henry appears in disguise and becomes captivated by Anne Bullen.

Buckingham is convicted. On his way toward execution, he asserts his loyalty, forgives his enemies, and warns the spectators against trusting friends who desert a falling man. Rumors now concern Henry's wish to end his marriage to Katherine, previously married to his brother Arthur. Courtiers suspect Wolsey's political designs, while others point to the king's attraction to another woman. Anne pities Katherine and declares that she would not want a crown, even as she receives the title Marchioness of Pembroke and a generous income.

At Blackfriars, Katherine appeals directly to Henry, defending more than twenty years as his faithful wife. She challenges Wolsey as a hostile judge, appeals to the pope, and leaves the court. Henry praises her character and publicly clears Wolsey of first raising the marital doubts. He attributes his concern to questions of legitimacy and the failure of their sons to survive. When Campeius adjourns proceedings, Henry privately condemns Roman delay and looks toward Cranmer for help. The cardinals later urge Katherine to place her cause in Henry's hands. She resists surrendering her title, fears betrayal, and eventually agrees to hear their counsel without withdrawing her devotion to the king.

Wolsey's position collapses when Henry discovers an inventory of his wealth among state papers and obtains his letter asking the pope to delay the divorce because of Henry's attachment to Anne. Wolsey had wanted a French marriage instead. The king has already secretly married Anne, and the nobles present accusations against the cardinal and announce proceedings to strip his possessions and protection. Confronting his fall, Wolsey recognizes the emptiness of worldly greatness. He urges the loyal Cromwell to serve Henry, reject ambition, and remain honest, lamenting that he served the king more zealously than God.

Anne's coronation is celebrated in an elaborate procession and a spectator's account of the ceremony. Katherine's marriage has been annulled, and she lies sick at Kimbolton. Griffith reports Wolsey's repentant death and balances her account of his faults with his learning and generosity. Katherine comes to honor his memory. In sleep she sees dancing figures offering garlands and understands the vision as a promise of heavenly peace. She sends Henry requests for their daughter's upbringing and her servants' welfare, then asks to be buried with the dignity of a queen.

As Anne gives birth to a daughter, Gardiner moves against Cranmer on charges of heresy. Henry privately gives Cranmer a ring with which to appeal to him. The council humiliates the archbishop by keeping him waiting and orders him to the Tower, but the ring halts the proceeding. Henry intervenes, rebukes the council, requires reconciliation, and appoints Cranmer godfather to the baby. Amid crowded public celebrations, Elizabeth returns from her christening. Cranmer prophesies her long, peaceful reign and the greatness of a male successor. Henry rejoices in this promised future and declares the day a holiday. The action ends with the infant's celebration, before the later lives and reigns described in the prophecy.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Buckingham's anger at Wolsey contrasts with Norfolk's advice to avoid a dangerous confrontation. Their discussion of the costly French meeting exposes resentment at the cardinal's influence, and Buckingham is arrested for treason before he can bring his accusations against Wolsey to Henry. Katherine persuades the king to cancel an oppressive levy; Wolsey immediately arranges to claim credit for the pardon. The surveyor's testimony portrays Buckingham as a potential usurper and assassin. Katherine warns that the witness lost his office and may bear a grudge, but Henry orders the duke's trial. Courtiers mock imported French fashions before attending Wolsey's feast. Henry arrives disguised among shepherd masquers, chooses Anne Bullen as his dancing partner, and reveals a strong attraction to her.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Gentlemen report Buckingham's conviction, and the condemned duke publicly declares his innocence and loyalty while forgiving those responsible. Discussion turns to the possible separation of Henry and Katherine. Nobles attribute the crisis to Wolsey's policies and Henry's attraction to another woman, while the king welcomes the papal judge Campeius. Anne expresses sympathy for Katherine and disclaims ambition, then receives a title and income from Henry. At the marriage hearing Katherine appeals to Henry's conscience, challenges Wolsey's impartiality, and leaves after appealing to the pope. Henry praises her virtues but explains his doubts about marrying his brother's widow and the succession. Campeius adjourns the court, leaving Henry impatient with Rome and hoping for Cranmer's return.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Katherine receives Wolsey and Campeius among her women, insisting on plain English and open discussion. Their advice to submit her cause to Henry seems to her a demand for ruin, and she refuses willingly to surrender her royal title. She finally accepts further counsel while reaffirming her love and prayers for Henry. Meanwhile Wolsey's enemies learn that the king has read his letter seeking delay of the divorce, and Henry discovers the cardinal's extraordinary wealth in a mistakenly enclosed inventory. Wolsey is ordered to surrender the great seal and faces forfeiture. His resistance gives way to recognition of his fall. Cromwell reports Anne's secret marriage and Cranmer's promotion; Wolsey advises him to serve honestly, abandon ambition, and learn from his master's ruin.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Spectators welcome Anne's coronation procession and describe its splendor, while reporting that Katherine's marriage has been annulled and she is ill at Kimbolton. Their conversation also establishes Cromwell's growing influence and the tension between Gardiner and Cranmer. At Kimbolton Griffith tells Katherine that Wolsey died repentant after illness interrupted his journey under arrest. She recalls his faults, then accepts Griffith's praise of his scholarship, benefactions, and humility in defeat. A vision of white-robed figures offering a garland accompanies her sleep; she wakes believing they promised eternal happiness. Visited by Caputius, she sends Henry a letter asking care for their daughter and faithful servants. She prepares for death and requests an honorable royal burial, leaving the stage still alive.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: While Anne struggles in childbirth, Gardiner boasts of the council's move against Cranmer. Henry warns the archbishop about his enemies and gives him a ring for an appeal if the council commits him. News arrives that Anne has borne a girl. Cranmer is kept waiting outside the council chamber, where Butts notices the insult and brings it to Henry's attention. Accused of spreading heresy and ordered to the Tower, Cranmer produces the ring. Henry intervenes, rebukes the councillors, requires them to embrace Cranmer, and makes him a godfather. Porters struggle with the crowd drawn to the christening. Elizabeth is presented in procession, and Cranmer foretells blessings under her and a male successor. Henry celebrates the prophecy and declares a holiday.

framing.label: Prologue
framing.summary: The speaker asks the audience to expect a serious history of power and suffering, to imagine its great figures as living people, and to respond with pity when their prominence gives way to misery. Spectacle is promised alongside the sorrowful story.

framing.label: Epilogue
framing.summary: The speaker jokes that no play can satisfy every spectator, especially those seeking sleep or attacks on the city. He appeals to sympathetic women to approve the virtuous woman portrayed and to encourage the men to applaud.
